title: Steve Jobs on Aesthetics, Mistakes, and Making Things Great (Moritz, 1984)
summary: In a May 1984 interview, Jobs says his taste is ordinary but his stubbornness isn't: making something great costs little extra beyond time and perseverance. He describes aesthetics as a trained eye refined by mistakes, and pushes for smaller, simpler, more precise products.

principles.text: Making something great costs little extra; it takes a bit more time and the willingness to persevere.
principles.quote: if you’re going to make something, it doesn’t take any more energy—and rarely does it take more money—to make it really great. All it takes is a little more time.

principles.text: Taste is refined by making mistakes.
principles.quote: Your aesthetics get better as you make mistakes.

principles.text: Good aesthetics come from a trained eye and instinct for what you see, like a singer's ear.
principles.quote: good aesthetics result from just your eye. An instinct of what you see, not so much what you do.

principles.text: Your taste isn't special; the edge is being stubborn about making things as good as they can be.
principles.quote: The difference is that I just get to be really stubborn about making things as good as we all know they can be.

principles.text: Smaller products allow more precise execution of form.
principles.quote: when you make things smaller, you have the ability to make them more precisely.

principles.text: Keep driving products toward radical simplicity.
principles.quote: we’re just getting simpler and simpler and simpler. Very, very simple.
